div.div: Some of the strongest attacks work by building across turns rather than landing in one prompt. Whether that is possible comes down to a single question: does the target keep the conversation, or do you have to hand it back every time?

div.div:
Every request is complete on its own, and it grows. The agent rebuilds the context from the history array each time and holds nothing between calls.
The field to get right
assistant_role the label this agent uses for its own messages in the history, often assistant.
Use it when the target is a standard stateless REST API with no session management of its own, which is the common case for anything built as a thin wrapper over a model.

div.div:
The target keeps the conversation behind a session id. The platform's only job is to read that id out of one response and put it back into the next request.
The two fields to get right
response_id_field the JSON path where the session id appears in the response
request_id_field the JSON path where it is injected on the next request
Use it when the agent manages its own history server-side, which includes both bridges in the appendix: each maps a session id onto an upstream conversation.

div.div: session_pre_process() creates the server-side session once per conversation, and context.session carries it into every later turn. It resets between conversations

div.style: display: flex; align-items: unsafe flex-start; justify-content: unsafe flex-start; width: 664px; height: 1px; padding-top: 769px; margin-left: 17px;
box-sizing: border-box; font-size: 0; text-align: left; color: #00294D;
display: inline-block; font-size: 12px; font-family: Helvetica; color: #00294D; line-height: 1.2; pointer-events: all; white-space: normal; word-wrap: normal;
div.b: Handing over the system prompt is the strongest thing you can do

div.style: display: flex; align-items: unsafe flex-start; justify-content: unsafe flex-start; width: 648px; height: 1px; padding-top: 789px; margin-left: 19px;
box-sizing: border-box; font-size: 0; text-align: left; color: #333333;
display: inline-block; font-size: 11px; font-family: Helvetica; color: #333333; line-height: 1.2; pointer-events: all; white-space: normal; word-wrap: normal;

div.div:
Filling in system_prompt on the target profile turns the run into
white-box testing, the most effective mode available. The attack
agent reads the instructions and the guardrails it has to get past,
and writes prompts aimed at those specific sentences.
Customers hesitate because it feels like handing over the keys.
The answer is that an attacker who finds a System Prompt Leak
gets it anyway, and the point of the exercise is to find out what
happens next.

div.style: display: flex; align-items: unsafe flex-start; justify-content: unsafe flex-start; width: 664px; height: 1px; padding-top: 769px; margin-left: 717px;
box-sizing: border-box; font-size: 0; text-align: left; color: #00294D;
display: inline-block; font-size: 12px; font-family: Helvetica; color: #00294D; line-height: 1.2; pointer-events: all; white-space: normal; word-wrap: normal;
div.b: Multi-turn is where the interesting failures are

div.style: display: flex; align-items: unsafe flex-start; justify-content: unsafe flex-start; width: 648px; height: 1px; padding-top: 789px; margin-left: 719px;
box-sizing: border-box; font-size: 0; text-align: left; color: #333333;
display: inline-block; font-size: 11px; font-family: Helvetica; color: #333333; line-height: 1.2; pointer-events: all; white-space: normal; word-wrap: normal;

div.div:
A target that refuses every single-turn attack can still be walked
into the same answer over four polite exchanges. Multi-Turn is
one of the nine Security subcategories for exactly that reason,
and it is the category a chatbot with good filters most often fails.
So a WebSocket target scanned on the native method is not
getting a complete assessment, however clean the report looks.
Say so before the customer reads a low risk score as an all-clear.
